previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease and severe peripheral vascular disease was admitted for a right below-the-knee amputation due to unrelenting pain and tissue necrosis from ischemia. Postoperatively, she developed cellulitis at the stump site, managed with intravenous antibiotics including vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole. Phantom limb pain was initially severe but improved with a ketamine drip and transition to oral analgesics. A second procedure was performed to place stents in the left superficial femoral artery and perform angioplasty on the right common iliac artery to improve circulation. Her anticoagulation was managed with a heparin drip while warfarin was restarted, though her INR remained subtherapeutic at discharge. She participated in physical therapy, was weaned off narcotics, and was discharged to extended care with plans for wound care, anticoagulation monitoring, and gradual tapering of oxycodone.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ y/o F with pMHx significant for CAD on ASA/Plavix,coumadin, 
CABG, ESRD on HD (TTHS), AVR, dCHF, right BKA presenting with 
epigastric tightness and shortness of breath. Tightness resolved 
by time patient presented to hospital, and breathing completely 
resolved s/p HD. Thought to be pulm edema in the setting of 
dCHF. Infectious and ischemic workup negative, PE eval deferred 
given improvement with HD, no hemodynamic compromise, current 
anticoagulation, and allergy to contrast dye. Concern for 
unstable angina, though less likely as pain was transient and 
completely resolved with reduction in volume and improvment in 
oxygenation/pulm edema. TTE showed LVEF >55% with LVH. 

# Shortness of breath/chest pressure
Ddx broad and in this patient, concern for PE (given AVR and 
subtherpeutic INR) vs. ACS (although CKMB neg x2) vs. flash pulm 
edema vs. dCHF exacerbation vs. unstable angina.  Low suspicion 
for PE and low wells score, although she did have surgery about 
a month ago. Low suspicion for ACS given neg CKMB, although she 
has an extensive cardiac history.  Her symptoms started acutely, 
making flash pulmonary edema a possibility,  She has no history 
of any lung disease. Could be acute on chronic CHF, as her 
weight is up, although again no clear cause as she has been 
attending dialysis

# Anti-coagulation/Mechanical Valve:
Pt is on coumadin for AVR; however, INR is 1.4 upon admission. 
Per patient, her INR had been supratherpeutic so coumadin was 
held for 3 days. Then found INR was ___ yesterday and she was 
given 5mg coumadin.

TRANSITIONAL ISSUES:
- Dyspnea/volume: Patient should discuss volume management with 
HD team and nephrologist to help prevent future volume 
overload/CHF exacerbation. 

-Chest pain: Concern for unstable angina, though less likely as 
pain was transient and completely resolved with reduction in 
volume and improvment in oxygenation/pulm edema. Should follow 
with cardiology for further evaluation. 

- Anticoagulation: Patient is being discharged with a 
subtherapeutic INR without bridge (cannot have enoxaparin given 
ESRD) as she has previously. She understands the risks and will 
be checking INR daily with daily communication with PCP for 
adjustments in coumadin dose. 

-Vascular: Patient should follow up with vascular surgery 
regarding plans for further surgery on lower extremities.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___, 

You were admitted to ___ with 
chest pain and shortness of breath. Evaluation for infection and 
heart attack were negative. You appeared to have extra fluid in 
your body and your symptoms improved drastically after removal 
of fluid at dialysis. You should weigh yourself every morning, 
call MD if weight goes up more than 3 lbs. As we discussed, you 
should discuss fluid management with your kidney doctor and 
dialysis team. You are at some increased risk of blood clot in 
the lungs given recent surgery and subtherapeutic INR, but given 
the risks of testing for blood clot, the fact that you are 
already on warfarin, and the drastic improvement with volume 
removal testing for blood clot was deferred. 

Your INR, a measurement of your anticoagulation on Coumadin, has 
been low since before your admission. We restarted your Coumadin 
on admission while anticoagulating with heparin. You should 
follow up with your daily INR checks and discuss dose 
adjustments with your doctor. As we discussed, there is some 
increased risk of blood clot and stroke with subtherapeutic INR, 
but you have been discharged under these conditions previously 
and will discuss with your doctor tomorrow. 

It was a pleasure caring for you, 

Your ___ Doctors
